usage: 운동 takes the object marker 을 because 하다 acts on it
subject marker 이 after a consonant
-고 싶어요 attaches to the verb 하-, not to the noun
좋아하다 is a verb 'to like', so its object takes 을/를
examples: 저는 매일 운동을 해요.
I exercise every day.
the everyday 운동하다 frame for a habit
살을 빼려고 요즘 운동을 시작했어요.
I started exercising lately to lose weight.
운동을 시작하다 = take up working out
헬스장에서 한 시간 동안 운동했더니 온몸이 뻐근해요.
After working out at the gym for an hour, my whole body is stiff.
real gym talk; 운동하다 contracted, with a result
nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') by analogy with 'make exercise' — Korean uses the light verb 하다; and remember the desire ending goes on the verb (운동하고 싶어요), never on the bare noun.

mistakes: Saying 운동을 만들어요 by translating 'do/make exercise' literally — 만들다 means physically craft something; the correct light verb is 하다, so 운동을 해요.
Attaching the want-ending to the noun as 운동 싶어요 — -고 싶다 only fastens to a verb stem, so it must be 운동하고 싶어요 / 운동을 하고 싶어요.
Using 운동들 to mean several workouts — 운동 is non-count here; say 운동을 여러 번 해요 or 자주 운동해요 instead.

usage: 보다 'see/watch' governs the object marker 를
subject marker 가 after a vowel
I want to watch a movie
-고 싶어요 on the verb 보-, with 를 on 영화
films are counted with the counter 편, not 개
examples: 주말에 영화를 봐요.
I watch a movie on the weekend.
simple habit with 보다
넷플릭스로 영화 한 편 보면서 쉬었어요.
I relaxed watching a movie on Netflix.
영화 + counter 편 + means-particle (으)로
이 영화 진짜 재밌으니까 꼭 영화관에서 봐.
This movie is really good, so be sure to see it at the theater.
casual 반말; 영화관 = cinema, 재밌다 colloquial
nuance: 영화 is Sino-Korean, 映畵 ('project-picture'), literally a projected image, and it is the standard word for a movie/film. It pairs with 보다 ('see/watch'), never 듣다 ('listen'), because film is something you view. A single film is counted with the bound noun 편 (영화 두 편 = two movies), not 개. Don't confuse 영화 with 드라마: 드라마 is a serialized TV series, while 영화 is a self-contained cinema film, so a Korean TV soap is a 드라마, not a 영화. The cinema building is 영화관 (or the loanword 극장). The classic English-speaker pitfall is letting 'a movie' steer you to the generic counter 개 (영화 한 개 sounds wrong) — use 편; and don't calque 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가다, since you say 영화(를) 보러 가다, 'go in order to watch a movie'.

Counting with 개 as in 영화 한 개 — films use the dedicated counter 편: 영화 한 편.
Translating 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가요 — Korean expresses purpose, so it is 영화를 보러 가요 ('go to watch a movie').

usage: 듣다 'hear/listen' takes 을; note ㄷ→ㄹ in 들어요
좋다 is an adjective; subject marker 이
좋아하다 (verb) governs an object with 을
틀다 = switch on/play a track from a device
examples: 저는 음악을 들어요.
I listen to music.
bare habit, 듣다 → 들어요
운동할 때 신나는 음악을 들으면 힘이 나요.
When I exercise, listening to upbeat music energizes me.
듣다 conditional 들으면; ㄷ-irregular
카페에서 잔잔한 음악을 틀어 놓으니 분위기가 좋네요.
With soft music playing in the café, the mood is nice.
틀어 놓다 = leave it playing in the background
nuance: 음악 is Sino-Korean, 音樂 ('sound-pleasure/joy'), and is the general word for music. Its everyday partner verb is 듣다 ('hear/listen'), which is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so 듣 + 어요 → 들어요 and 듣 + 으면 → 들으면 — memorize this because beginners often write the wrong ❌들다. Distinguish 음악 from 노래: 노래 is a specific 'song' you can sing (with words and a tune), while 음악 is music as a whole, including instrumental pieces, so background café music is 음악, not 노래. Two near-verbs differ too — 듣다 is to receive sound, but 틀다 is to switch a track on from a device. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 ('watch') because you 'watch a music video' in English; for plain audio say 음악을 들어요, and avoid the false stem 들다 — the dictionary form is 듣다.

Using 만들다 for 'make/play music' on a device — to start a track you 틀다, e.g. 음악을 틀어요.

usage: 부르다 'to sing' (르-irregular) is the precise verb
듣다 → 들어요 for receiving the song
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 부르- → 부를 수 있어요
songs are counted with 곡, not 개
examples: 저는 노래를 잘 불러요.
I sing well.
부르다 → 불러요 (르-irregular doubling)
친구 생일이라 다 같이 생일 노래를 불렀어요.
It was my friend's birthday, so we all sang the birthday song.
past 불렀어요; 다 같이 = all together
노래방에서 한 곡 부르고 나니까 스트레스가 풀렸어요.
After singing a song at the karaoke room, my stress melted away.
노래방 culture; counter 곡; -고 나니까
nuance: 노래 is a native Korean word for a 'song' — a tune with lyrics you can perform — counted with the bound noun 곡 (노래 두 곡). The most natural verb is 부르다 ('to sing'), a 르-irregular: the stem doubles the ㄹ before a vowel, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and 부르 + 었어요 → 불렀어요. The casual frame 노래를 하다 ('do a song') exists and means to sing, but 노래를 부르다 is more precise and common. Don't blur 노래 with 음악: 음악 is music in general (including instrumentals), while 노래 specifically has a singer and words. Karaoke is 노래방 ('song room'), a core social ritual. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 말하다 ('say/speak') because we 'say the words of a song' — singing is 부르다, never 말하다; and don't translate 'sing a song' twice over as ❌노래를 노래해요, which is redundant — just 노래를 불러요.

usage: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 추- → 출 수 있어요
examples: 저는 춤을 잘 춰요.
I dance well.
추다 → 춰요 (우 + 어 contracts to 워)
무대에서 아이돌처럼 춤을 추니까 다들 환호했어요.
When I danced like an idol on stage, everyone cheered.
춤을 추다 in action; -니까 sequence
요즘 방송댄스 배우는데, 춤 동작이 생각보다 어려워요.
I'm learning K-pop dance lately, and the moves are harder than I expected.
춤 + 동작 = dance move; -는데 background
nuance: 춤 is a native noun for 'dance', and Korean uses a cognate-verb construction: the verb 추다 ('to dance') pairs only with 춤, giving 춤을 춰요 (추 + 어요 → 춰요, the 우+어 fuses to 워). This 'cognate object' pattern — noun and verb sharing a root — also appears in 잠을 자다 (sleep a sleep) and 꿈을 꾸다 (dream a dream), so learn it as a set. The dictionary form is 춤추다, written solid. The English-speaker pitfall is the reflex 춤을 해요 with the all-purpose light verb 하다 — that is unnatural for dance; you must use the specific verb 추다. Also, while 춤 covers dancing broadly, a single dance 'piece/move' is better called a 동작 (motion) or a specific genre (발레 ballet, 힙합 hip-hop), so don't try to count individual dances with 개. Note 멋있다 (cool) is the natural compliment, not 예쁘다.

mistakes: Saying 춤을 해요 with the generic light verb — dance requires its cognate verb 추다, so 춤을 춰요.
Writing the contraction wrong as 추어요 left unfused — colloquial Korean contracts 추 + 어요 to 춰요.
Splitting the dictionary form as two words 춤 추다 in the lexicon sense — the verb 'to dance' is the single word 춤추다 (though 춤을 추다 as object+verb is fine).

usage: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 그리- → 그릴 수 있어요
flat artworks are counted with 장 (sheets)
examples: 저는 그림을 그려요.
I draw pictures.
cognate pair 그림/그리다
조카가 크레용으로 그림을 그려서 냉장고에 붙였어요.
My niece drew a picture with crayons, so I stuck it on the fridge.
그리다 → 그려서; everyday scene
이 화가의 그림은 색감이 정말 예술이에요.
This painter's paintings have truly artistic colors.
화가 = painter; 그림 as fine-art painting
nuance: 그림 is a native noun covering both a 'drawing' and a 'painting', formed from the verb 그리다 ('to draw/paint') — another cognate noun-verb pair, so 그림을 그리다 literally means 'draw a drawing'. A flat artwork is counted with 장 (sheets): 그림 한 장. Korean does not split 'draw' vs 'paint' lexically the way English does; 그리다 covers both pencil sketches and oil paintings, and you specify the medium (색연필로, 물감으로) if needed. The verb 그리다 also figuratively means to 'picture/long for' something (고향을 그리다, to yearn for home), but the everyday hobby sense is making art. The English-speaker pitfall is using 만들다 ('make') because we say 'make a drawing' — Korean uses the cognate verb 그리다, so say 그림을 그려요. Don't confuse 그림 with 사진 (a photograph): 그림 is hand-made art, 사진 is a photo you 찍다 ('take').

Counting with 개 (그림 한 개) — flat works on paper take 장: 그림 한 장.

usage: 가다 'go'; the most idiomatic frame, 여행을 가다
light verb 하다 → 여행하다, more formal feel
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 여행
examples: 방학에 여행을 가요.
I go on a trip during the vacation.
여행을 가다, time particle 에
내년에 유럽으로 배낭여행을 떠나려고 돈을 모으고 있어요.
I'm saving money to set off backpacking around Europe next year.
떠나다 = set off; 배낭여행 compound
이번 제주도 여행 정말 좋았어, 다음엔 같이 가자.
This Jeju trip was really great; let's go together next time.
casual 반말; 여행 as a concrete trip
nuance: 여행 is Sino-Korean, 旅行 ('journey-go'), meaning travel or a trip. The single most natural verb is 가다 — 여행을 가다 ('go on a trip') — while 여행하다 (with light verb 하다) also works but feels a touch more formal/written. Distinguish 여행 from 출장: 출장 is a business trip you're sent on for work, whereas 여행 is travel for pleasure or sightseeing, so don't call a work assignment a 여행. A traveler is 여행자/여행객 and an overseas trip is 해외여행. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing 보다 ('see') because tourists 'go sightseeing' — to travel you 가다 or 하다, not 보다 (sightseeing specifically is 구경하다 or 관광하다). Also note destination takes (으)로/에 (제주도로 여행을 가다), and beginners often drop the particle on 여행 itself — keep 여행을 가다.

Marking the destination with only 에 and no movement sense, e.g. 부산에 여행이에요 — say 부산으로/에 여행을 가요 to express going there.

usage: Sino-noun + 하다; the standard frame 독서하다
examples: 저는 자기 전에 독서를 해요.
I read before going to bed.
독서하다 for a tidy habit statement
제 취미는 독서라서 주말마다 도서관에 가요.
My hobby is reading, so I go to the library every weekend.
독서 + 도서관 share the 書/도 imagery
요즘 일이 바빠서 통 독서를 못 했네요.
I've been so busy with work lately that I've hardly read at all.
통 + 못 했다 = hardly did; reflective tone
nuance: 독서 is Sino-Korean, 讀書 ('read-book'), literally 'reading books', and it is a slightly formal, hobby-survey word — it's what you write when asked 취미가 뭐예요?, answering 독서예요. Because it already contains 書 ('book'), 독서 implies reading books specifically, so for casual everyday speech Koreans usually switch to the plain native verb phrase 책을 읽다 ('read a book') — 책 읽는 거 좋아해요 sounds far more natural in conversation than 독서를 좋아해요, which can feel stiff. It pairs with 하다 (독서하다), not 보다 ('watch'), even though English sometimes blurs 'read' and 'look at'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 (because you 'look at' a page) — reading text is 읽다, and the noun is 독서를 하다. Don't try to give 독서 an object like ❌소설을 독서해요; if you name what you read, drop the Sino-noun and say 소설을 읽어요.

mistakes: Saying 독서를 봐요 from 'look at a book' — reading is 읽다; the noun frame is 독서를 해요.

Using stiff 독서를 해요 in casual chat — among friends the natural phrasing is 책 읽어요 / 책 읽는 거 좋아해요.

usage: light verb 등산하다, the activity itself
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 등산
examples: 주말마다 등산을 해요.
I go hiking every weekend.
등산하다 for a routine
아버지는 친구들이랑 북한산으로 등산을 가셨어요.
My dad went hiking up Bukhansan with his friends.
honorific 가셨어요; 으로 destination
정상까지 등산하는 데 세 시간이나 걸렸어요.
It took a whole three hours to hike to the summit.
등산하다; -는 데 + 이나 emphasis
nuance: 등산 is Sino-Korean, 登山 ('climb-mountain'), specifically going up a mountain on foot, and it pairs with 가다 (등산을 가다) or 하다 (등산하다). It is culturally huge — weekend 등산 with proper gear is a beloved pastime, especially for middle-aged and older Koreans. Distinguish 등산 from 산책: 산책 is a light, flat stroll (a walk in the park or neighborhood), while 등산 implies real uphill climbing of a mountain, so an evening walk is a 산책, not 등산. Also note 하이킹 (loanword) overlaps but 등산 is the everyday native-feeling choice. The English-speaker pitfall is using 타다 ('ride') because we 'climb' mountains and 타다 can mean 'climb onto' a vehicle — for hiking on your own feet you 가다/하다, never 타다 (you'd only 타다 a cable car, 케이블카를 타다). Mark the mountain as a destination with (으)로/에: 산으로 등산을 가요.

usage: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on the verb 하-
examples: 저는 여름에 수영을 해요.
I swim in summer.
수영하다, seasonal habit
어렸을 때 수영을 배워서 지금도 잘해요.
I learned to swim as a kid, so I'm still good at it.
수영을 배우다 → 배워서; ability
수영장에서 한 시간 동안 수영하니까 배가 너무 고파요.
After swimming for an hour at the pool, I'm so hungry.
수영장; 수영하다; result with -니까
nuance: 수영 is Sino-Korean, 水泳 ('water-swim'), and means swimming as an activity; it pairs with the light verb 하다 (수영하다, 수영을 해요). A swimming pool is 수영장 ('swim-place'). Because 수영 names the whole activity, you don't use it for one isolated stroke — 수영을 해요 covers the act of swimming generally. Don't confuse the partner verbs across water sports: you 수영하다 (swim under your own power) but you 타다 ('ride') a surfboard or jet ski. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that — reaching for 타다 because many water/sport activities in English are 'rides', or because Korean uses 타다 for 스키 (스키를 타다, to ski) and 스케이트 (스케이트를 타다, to skate). Swimming is NOT one of those: it is 수영하다, never ❌수영을 타다. Note the contrast 스키를 타다 vs 수영을 하다 — sports that 'mount/ride' equipment take 타다, but body-only activities like swimming and exercise take 하다.

usage: 있다 'to have/exist' takes the subject marker 가
I started it as a hobby
취미로 = 'as a hobby', means/role particle 로
topic 는 to name your hobby
examples: 취미가 뭐예요?
What is your hobby?
the standard ice-breaker; 가, not 를
제 취미는 영화 보기예요.
My hobby is watching movies.
verb → noun with -기: 보다 → 보기
취미로 시작한 요리가 이제는 거의 직업이 됐어요.
Cooking, which I started as a hobby, has now almost become a job.
취미로; relative clause; 이/가 되다
nuance: 취미 is Sino-Korean, 趣味 ('interest-taste'), and means a hobby or personal interest. It famously opens small talk: 취미가 뭐예요? — and note it takes 가 there (existence/identity), so a frequent error is ❌취미를 있어요 instead of 취미가 있어요, because 있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb taking 을/를. To turn an activity into a named hobby, Korean nominalizes the verb with -기: 보다 → 영화 보기 ('movie-watching'), 모으다 → 우표 모으기 ('stamp-collecting'); answering 제 취미는 영화 보기예요 is the model pattern. Distinguish 취미 from 관심: 관심 is broader 'interest/attention' (관심이 있어요 = I'm interested in it), whereas 취미 is specifically a leisure activity you do for fun. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 있다 into a 'have'-with-object frame (취미를 있어요) — use 취미가 있어요; and don't say ❌취미를 해요 for 'do a hobby' — name the activity itself (영화를 봐요) or say 취미를 즐겨요.

usage: light verb 낚시하다 for the activity
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 낚시
examples: 아버지는 낚시를 좋아하세요.
My father likes fishing.
honorific 좋아하세요; 낚시 as hobby
주말에 바다로 낚시를 가서 광어를 두 마리 잡았어요.
I went sea-fishing at the weekend and caught two flatfish.
낚시를 가다 + 잡다; counter 마리
밤낚시는 조용해서 좋은데 모기가 너무 많아요.
Night fishing is nice because it's quiet, but there are way too many mosquitoes.
밤낚시 compound; -는데 contrast
nuance: 낚시 is a native noun meaning fishing (with rod and hook) as a pastime, pairing with 가다 (낚시를 가다) or 하다 (낚시하다). Spelling and sound are tricky: the ㄲ cluster means it is written 낚시 but pronounced [낙씨], and the fish-hook itself is 낚싯바늘 — beginners often misspell it ❌낙시. Distinguish the activity 낚시 from the bare act of catching: 잡다 ('to catch/grab') is what you do to the fish (물고기를 잡다), while 낚시(를 하다) is the whole sport of angling, so 'I caught a fish' is 물고기를 잡았어요, but 'I go fishing (as a hobby)' is 낚시를 가요/해요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 잡다 alone to mean 'go fishing' — 잡다 just means grab/catch and needs an object; for the recreational activity use 낚시를 하다. Mark the spot with (으)로/에서: 바다로 낚시를 가다, 강에서 낚시하다.
